question: Intesa Sanpaolo’s complaint to Consob – Italy’s financial markets regulatory and supervisory authority – contesting the correctness of the announced Monte dei Paschi di Siena (MPS) exchange offer for Banco BPM and Banca Generali highlights serious problems in the application of EU legislation on financial markets1.

Specifically, the transaction raises serious doubts as to compliance with Article 9 of Directive 2004/25/EC (the Takeover Directive) in relation to the passivity rule (the obligation of management bodies to refrain from defensive actions that could run counter to the objectives of the offer) and with the obligations of timely disclosure of inside information laid down in Regulation (EU) No 596/2014 (the Market Abuse Regulation – MAR).

In addition to undermining financial stability, such conduct risks breaching the principles of investor protection and transparency set out in the MiFID II Directive (2014/65/EU), to the detriment of small savers. In view of the above: 1.
Does the Commission consider MPS’s conduct to be a circumvention of the passivity rule within the meaning of Article 9 of Directive 2004/25/EC?
How does it intend to ask the European Securities and Markets Authority to confirm whether there have been breaches of the MAR (Regulation (EU) No 596/2014) rules on correct market information?
What urgent steps will it take to strengthen MiFID II safeguards to protect small shareholders exposed to potential market distortion manoeuvres?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (30.10.2026) Based on the information currently available and the ongoing investigations, the Commission may not express at this stage a view on whether Article 9 of Directive 2004/25/EC on takeover bids1 (the Takeover Directive) or Regulation (EU) No 596/2014 (the Market Abuse Regulation (MAR))2 have been infringed.

The Commission understands that Intesa Sanpaolo filed a complaint on 26 August 2026 with the Italian national authority competent for financial markets (CONSOB), which has the primary responsibility for assessing and deciding whether the Takeover Directive or the MAR have been infringed. That investigation is ongoing.

The European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) is an independent EU agency which disposes of several tools to ensure consistent, efficient and effective application of EU regulation of securities markets. Given the stage of the investigations, it is premature for the Commission to request ESMA to take any specific action.

Directive 2014/65/EU on Markets in Financial Instruments (MiFID II)3 sets out investor protection rules that investment firms distributing financial products to investors must follow. Those rules have recently been enhanced by the Retail Investment Strategy4.
Before any further legislative amendments can be tabled in this area, it would be appropriate to implement and assess the impact of the recently agreed measures.

1 OJ L 142, 30.4.2004, pp. 12–23: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2004/25/oj. 2 OJ L 173, 12.6.2014, pp. 1–61: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2014/596/oj. 3 OJ L 173, 12.6.2014, p. 349-496: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2014/65/oj. 4 https://finance.ec.europa.eu/publications/retail-investment-strategy_en.
